title: The Man Who Walked to the River
subtitle: Balarama Refuses to Take Sides and Departs for the Saraswati Tirthas
story:
While the Pandava camp rang with the order to draw up for battle, one man among the Vrishnis would take no part in it, and he was Krishna's own elder brother.

The decision had been made. When Krishna had finished speaking, all the kings there present had looked at Yudhishthira's face, and Yudhishthira, understanding them, had given the word with Bhima and Arjuna and the twins: draw up the troops in battle array. A great uproar rose amongst the Pandava army, and all the soldiers were filled with joy. King Yudhishthira the Just, however, beholding the impending slaughter of those that deserved not to be slain, began to sigh deeply. That for the sake of which I accepted an exile into the woods, he said, and for which I suffered so much misery, that great calamity overtaketh us of a set purpose. How shall we fight with those reverend superiors whom we on no account can slay? Kings rose from their seats and took up their arms; the two great hosts arranged themselves across Kurukshetra. In the middle of that gathering of warriors, Balarama stood apart.

He was unwilling to fight against either the Pandavas or Duryodhana. Both armies held men he had known all his life, and he would raise his arm against neither. Yet his refusal was not a withdrawal from the quarrel of his own heart. As regards myself, he declared, I dare not cast my eyes on the world without Krishna on my side. It is for this that I follow whatever Krishna seeketh to achieve.

He followed Krishna's cause, then, without reservation, and the words he left behind were not the words of a man washing his hands of the quarrel. But following it was not the same as standing on the field to watch it carried out. I shall now repair to the tirtha of the Saraswati for ablutions, Balarama said, for I shall not be able to behold with indifference the destruction of the Kauravas.

So, while the kings armed themselves and the soldiers raised their joyful uproar and the two hosts settled into their places, Balarama turned his back on the field. He walked to the Saraswati, the sacred river of the sages, to its holy fords, places of ablution and prayer where pilgrims came to be cleansed, and there he would bathe and pray. A warrior leaving the war he could neither join nor watch: his refusal to fight was no judgment against either army, but the only position left to a man who loved both sides and could not bear to see one of them destroyed.

The war would be fought without him, and the brothers of the Vrishni race would part at the edge of it. Behind Balarama, the greatest war of the age gathered itself. Before him lay the quiet fords of the Saraswati, where the water asked nothing of any man. He had chosen the only side left to him: the side of neither army, and of the one cause he could not abandon.
reflection: Balarama's withdrawal is not indifference — he follows Krishna's cause even as he refuses to witness its cost. The story is a quiet acknowledgment that devotion and kinship can pull in different directions, and that sometimes the honest answer to an unbearable war is to walk away from it and let the water carry what the field cannot.
next_story_tease: On the morning of battle, Krishna would bid Arjuna hymn Durga for victory.
hero_scene: At the edge of the Pandava camp, Balarama walks away from the field with his back to the drawn-up armies, his staff in hand, the river Saraswati glittering ahead of him while banners and dust rise behind.
